meta.title: Unit 1 Lab, Checkpoint 1: Density and Measurement

modules.intro: Measure the volume and mass of every required sample yourself. Choose the volume technique that fits each sample's geometry and hold the precision your instruments actually give you. Everything you need to do this is written below.
modules.title: Measurement

blocks.content:
### What you are doing

Six numbered samples are in front of you. Each one is a real engineering material with its label removed. Your job is to measure each sample carefully enough that its density tells you what it is.

You are not guessing. Density is mass divided by volume, and every material has its own. Measure well and the number does the identifying for you.

### The six candidates

Every sample is one of these:

| Status | Material |
|---|---|
| Required | ASTM 1018 steel |
| Required | 6061 aluminum |
| Required | 304 stainless steel (ASTM A276) |
| Required | Polycarbonate |
| Bonus | ASTM B16 brass |
| Bonus | Ti-6Al-4V titanium |

Samples 5 and 6 are bonus. They earn IDEA Coins, not points. Attempt them only after 1 through 4 are finished.

### Units, before anything else

**Work in grams and centimeters.** Published density is reported in g/cm3. Record mass in kilograms or volume in mm3 and your comparison will be off by a factor of 1000.

1 mL of displaced water = 1 cm3 exactly.

### Step 1. Choose your volume technique

Look at the sample's shape.

- If it is a shape with a volume formula, use the **dimensional** technique. Record DIM.
- If it is irregular, or too small to measure cleanly, use **displacement**. Record DISP.

### Step 2a. Dimensional technique

Measure with the caliper, then apply the formula for that shape.

| Shape | What to measure | Volume |
|---|---|---|
| Rectangular bar | length L, width W, height H | V = L x W x H |
| Round rod | diameter D, length L | V = pi x (D/2)^2 x L |
| Tube | outside D, inside d, length L | V = pi x ((D/2)^2 - (d/2)^2) x L |
| Sheet or plate | length L, width W, thickness T | V = L x W x T |

Measure every dimension twice. If two readings disagree, re-seat the caliper and take a third.

### Step 2b. Displacement technique

1. Fill the graduated cylinder partway. Read the starting level and write it down.
2. Slide the sample in. Do not drop it.
3. Read the new level.
4. Volume = ending level minus starting level.

Read at the bottom of the curve the water makes, with your eye level with the line.

If the sample floats it is less dense than water, which is already useful information. Hold it under with a thin rod and note that you did.

### Step 3. Mass

Zero the scale with nothing on it, place the sample, and record the reading in grams.

### Step 4. Significant figures

Write down every digit the instrument shows you, including trailing zeros.

If the caliper reads 12.70 mm, write 12.70 mm. Writing 12.7 mm throws away a digit the instrument actually measured. If the scale reads 18.40 g, write 18.40 g.

Your calculated volume should not carry more digits than the measurements it came from.

### Worked example

A round rod. The caliper reads D = 1.270 cm and L = 4.000 cm.

    V = pi x (1.270 / 2)^2 x 4.000
    V = pi x (0.635)^2 x 4.000
    V = pi x 0.4032 x 4.000
    V = 5.067 cm3

The scale reads 18.24 g.

That is everything Module 1 needs for one sample. The density itself comes in Module 2.

levels.label: Complete
levels.descriptor: All four required samples have a recorded shape, a named volume technique, every measurement that technique needs, a volume in cm3, and a mass in grams.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.descriptor: All four required samples are measured, with one sample missing its shape, its named technique, or one required dimension.

levels.label: Developing
levels.descriptor: Two or three samples are completely measured, or all four are present with volume or mass missing on more than one.

levels.label: Absent
levels.descriptor: Fewer than two samples are measured, or no measurements are recorded.

levels.label: Complete
levels.descriptor: Every dimension and mass is recorded to the full resolution the instrument reads, trailing zeros are retained where they are significant, and the calculated volume carries the same precision as its inputs, on all four samples.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.descriptor: Recorded to instrument resolution on all four samples, with precision dropped or digits added beyond the instrument's reading on one or two individual values.

levels.label: Developing
levels.descriptor: Recorded to instrument resolution on two or three samples, or resolution is correct throughout but values are rounded to different precision from one sample to the next.

levels.label: Absent
levels.descriptor: Values are recorded without regard to instrument resolution, or fewer than two samples carry usable precision.

modules.intro: Calculate density from your own measurements, compare each result against a published value you look up yourself, and state a first identification for every required sample based on that comparison.
modules.title: Density, Comparison, and Hypothesis

blocks.content:
### Step 5. Calculate density

    density = mass / volume

Use your own numbers from Module 1, and write the division out rather than only the answer.

Continuing the worked example: 18.24 g / 5.067 cm3 = 3.600 g/cm3

### Step 6. Look up the published value

Published property values come from **MatWeb**, at matweb.com. OnlineMetals, Industrial Metal Supply, and McMaster-Carr sell material and list prices. They are not property databases, and some carry no property data for plastics at all.

Finding a density on MatWeb:

1. Search the material name, for example "6061-T6 aluminum".
2. Open an entry from the results list.
3. Find the Physical Properties section near the top.
4. Density is listed in g/cc, which is the same thing as g/cm3.
5. Write the value down and name the entry you used. Alloys have several entries for different tempers and conditions, and the numbers differ between them.

Look up the candidates your measurement lands near, not all six.

### Step 7. Percent error

    percent error = |measured - published| / published x 100

The bars mean absolute value, so drop the minus sign if you get one.

Continuing the example, against a published value of 3.55 g/cm3:

    |3.600 - 3.55| / 3.55 x 100 = 0.05 / 3.55 x 100 = 1.4%

A percent error of a few percent means your measurement and the published value agree. A percent error in the hundreds or thousands is a units problem, not a discovery. Check grams and cm3 before you check anything else.

### Step 8. State your hypothesis

For each sample write which material you think it is, and give both numbers: your measured density and the published density you matched it to.

Density will not settle everything. Two aluminum alloys sit within a fraction of a percent of each other, and 1018 steel and 304 stainless are within a few percent. If two candidates are both plausible, say so and name both. Monday's lab gives you a second kind of evidence to break the tie.

The most accurate results in the class earn IDEA Coins.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.descriptor: Density is computed for all four samples with the division shown on two or three of them, or shown on all four with one arithmetic error.

levels.label: Developing
levels.descriptor: Density is computed for two or three samples, or all four are given as results with no division shown anywhere.

levels.label: Absent
levels.descriptor: Fewer than two densities are computed, or the units are not mass over volume.

levels.label: Complete
levels.descriptor: All four required samples are compared against a published value with the source entry named, and percent error is computed for each.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.descriptor: All four are compared with percent error computed, with the source unnamed on one or more, or three of the four are complete.

levels.label: Absent
levels.descriptor: Fewer than three samples are compared against a published value, or no percent error is computed.

levels.label: Complete
levels.descriptor: An identification is named for each of the four required samples, and each names both the measured density and the published density it was matched to.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.descriptor: An identification is named for all four samples, with the supporting density values missing on one or more of them.

levels.label: Absent
levels.descriptor: Fewer than four samples are identified, or identifications are given with no reference to density.
